notes.title: Start here: a Notion-style workspace in Next.js
notes.body:
This project is a Notion-style workspace: nested pages, blocks of content on each page, comments, search, version history and export. It is a Next.js app with a Zustand store in the browser, API routes on the server, and a single SQLite database. The architecture guide calls it a strong MVP with deliberate shortcuts (for example one seeded workspace and no auth).

Suggested reading order (from `_learning/01-LEARNING-PATH.md`):

1. `_learning/00-ARCHITECTURE.md`: what the app is, who it is for, and which file owns which job.
2. The learning path chapters in order. Each chapter lists per-file guides under `_learning/guides/`, starting with small utility files and ending with the big UI component.
3. `_learning/03-PATTERNS.md`: patterns used well, then anti-patterns and risks. It is "intentionally honest".
4. `_learning/02-GLOSSARY.md` whenever a term is new.

Almost every quiz in this pack asks what one store action or API route does in a specific case. Read `src/lib/workspaceStore.js` and `src/app/api/workspace/route.js` with a concrete example in mind.

excerpts.quote: The app is currently a strong MVP, not a fully hardened production system.
Use this order. It starts with easiest files and builds toward the most complex one.

notes.title: How the store's actions change state
notes.body:
`src/lib/workspaceStore.js` is the app's central store, built with Zustand. Each action is a function that calls `set(...)` with a callback. The callback receives the current state and returns **only the parts that change**; returning `{}` means "change nothing". For every action, note each branch and what it returns, including any branch that returns an empty object.

Two habits make these actions easy to read:

- **Copy, then change.** Arrays and objects are copied first (`[...list]`, `{ ...state.blocksByPage }`), then the copy is edited, so the old state is never mutated.
- **Small array idioms.** You will see `filter` to remove items, `findIndex` to locate one, `splice` to insert at a position, and `slice` to take part of a list. For each, check what happens when the item you look for is not there.

For each action you read, write one concrete example input and the exact output. The patterns guide calls this store "centralized state", and its last pattern explains how the store merges state arriving from another tab.

excerpts.quote: One store (`useWorkspaceStore`) holds core UI state and mutation actions.
`src/lib/workspaceStore.js`: client-side app state and state mutation actions.

notes.title: Persistence: one JSON document per workspace
notes.body:
On the server, the whole workspace (pages, blocks, comments, activity log and more) is stored as **one JSON blob** in a SQLite table, one row per workspace. The `/api/workspace` route loads and saves that blob; a separate `/api/workspace/version` route saves and restores page versions.

This is simple and fast to build, and the patterns guide discusses it in its anti-patterns section. When reading the PUT handler, list each field of the stored state and trace where its final value comes from, and read what the SQL upsert does when a row already exists. Then ask what happens when two tabs save one after the other.

The app also syncs between browser tabs using `BroadcastChannel`, and keeps an offline queue in IndexedDB. The patterns guide describes the tab-to-tab merge rule and adds a caveat paragraph. Read both, then read `applyRemoteState` itself before the quizzes on remote state.

excerpts.quote: - `src/lib/sqlite.js`: SQLite bootstrap, schema creation, data read/write helpers. - `src/lib/offlineStore.js`: IndexedDB queue + draft storage for offline mode.

readMore.why: Full-blob persistence and fake realtime scope, with suggested fixes.

notes.title: Where addBlock puts a block when its anchor is gone
notes.body:
The key is right: at the end of the page. With an `afterBlockId` given, `addBlock` computes `list.findIndex((block) => block.id === afterBlockId)`. If that id no longer exists, `findIndex` returns `-1`. The next line checks `index < 0 || index === list.length - 1` and, in either case, calls `list.push(nextBlock)`, adding the block at the end. Only a found anchor that is not the last block uses `splice(index + 1, 0, nextBlock)` to insert right after it.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Ignored": the action always creates `nextBlock` and returns a new list.
- "After the first block": there is no fallback to the first block.
- "At the start, -1 + 1 = 0": that would happen only if the code spliced at `index + 1` without checking; the `index < 0` test sends it to `push` first.

excerpts.quote: const index = afterBlockId ? list.findIndex((block) => block.id === afterBlockId) : list.length - 1;
if (index < 0 || index === list.length - 1) { list.push(nextBlock); } else { list.splice(index + 1, 0, nextBlock);

notes.title: How the activity log stays at 200
notes.body:
The key is right: 200 entries; the new activity is appended and `slice(-200)` drops the oldest. The PUT handler builds `activities` as a new array: all existing entries, then one new entry for this save. Then it calls `.slice(-200)`. A negative argument to `slice` counts from the end, so it keeps the **last** 200 items. With 200 existing plus 1 new, that is 201 items, and the one cut off is the first, the oldest.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Reset to just the new entry": nothing clears the list.
- "The new activity is discarded": it is added before slicing, and slicing keeps the end, where the new entry is.
- "201, no limit": the `slice(-200)` is the limit.

notes.title: Why a child of a deleted page vanishes from the sidebar
notes.body:
The key is right: no, Q does not appear, because the recursion only goes through pages that are not deleted. `buildPageTree(pages, parentId)` keeps pages whose `parentId` matches **and** whose `isDeleted` is false, then calls itself for each survivor to find its children. At the level where P lives, P is filtered out. So `buildPageTree(pages, P.id)` is never called, and Q, whose parent is P, is never reached. Q still exists in `pages`; it is just unreachable from the visible tree while P is in the trash.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Promoted to the root": Q's `parentId` is still P, so it never matches the root level (`null`).
- "Q's own flag is false, so it is kept": Q's flag would matter only if the recursion reached Q's level.
- "Nested under a greyed-out P": deleted pages are filtered out, not drawn differently.

notes.title: How old presence and typing entries may get
notes.body:
The key is right: presence up to 13000 ms, typing indicators up to 3000 ms. Both prune functions work the same way: for each entry, keep it if `now - updatedAt <= maxAgeMs`. The difference is the default: `prunePresence(maxAgeMs = 13000)` and `pruneTyping(maxAgeMs = 3000)`. So "this person is on the page" survives up to 13 seconds without an update, while "this person is typing" disappears after 3 seconds. That makes sense: typing is a short-lived signal.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Both survive until reload": the prune functions remove stale entries while the page is open.
- "Typing outlives presence": the numbers are the other way round.
- "Both 13000 ms": typing has its own, shorter default.

notes.title: Why remote state with an equal timestamp changes nothing
notes.body:
The key is right: nothing changes, because remote state is applied only when it is strictly newer. `applyRemoteState` turns both `meta.updatedAt` values into numbers and returns `{}` (no change) if the remote one is NaN or `remoteUpdatedAt <= localUpdatedAt`. Equal counts as "not newer", so it is ignored. The patterns guide adds a real consequence: edits never bump `meta.updatedAt` on the client, so two tabs loaded from the same save carry equal timestamps and drop each other's messages.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Remote always replaces local": the guard stops it unless remote is newer.
- "Only pages and blocks replaced": when it does apply, it replaces every listed collection, comments included.
- "Merged key by key": there is no merge; when newer, collections are replaced wholesale.

excerpts.quote: Two tabs loaded from the same saved state therefore carry equal timestamps and drop each other's state messages

notes.title: What restoring a page version changes
notes.body:
The key is right: it overlays page X with the snapshot's page and blocks, and bumps `meta.updatedAt`. The PATCH handler loads the saved version and the current workspace, finds X by id, and then:

- sets `state.pages[pageIndex]` to the current page, overwritten by the snapshot's page fields, with a fresh `updatedAt`;
- replaces `state.blocksByPage[X]` with the snapshot's blocks;
- sets `state.meta.updatedAt` to now and saves the workspace.

Nothing else is touched.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Creates a new page next to X": it writes into X's existing slot.
- "Only the title": the snapshot page fields and the blocks are both restored.
- "Rolls back the whole workspace": only X's page entry and X's blocks change; other pages stay as they are.

excerpts.quote: state.pages[pageIndex] = { ...state.pages[pageIndex], ...version.snapshot.page, updatedAt: new Date().toISOString(), }; state.blocksByPage[version.pageId] = version.snapshot.blocks || [];

notes.title: Why two tabs' saves lose one tab's work
notes.body:
The key is right: the server keeps tab B's whole state, so A's rename is lost. Each PUT sends the **entire** workspace. The route builds `nextState` from it and calls `upsertWorkspaceState`, whose SQL is `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT(workspace_id) DO UPDATE SET state_json = excluded.state_json`: the stored blob is replaced by the new one. Tab B's copy still has page X's old title, so saving it overwrites A's rename. The patterns guide lists this under full-blob persistence: hard concurrent-write conflict handling.

Why the others are wrong:
- "B is rejected by a version check": the route has no version check; it only validates the basic shape.
- "Merged page by page": nothing merges; the blob is replaced.
- "Flagged as a conflict": no conflict detection exists on the server.

excerpts.quote: ON CONFLICT(workspace_id) DO UPDATE SET state_json = excluded.state_json,
Hard diffing and concurrent write conflict handling.

notes.title: What opening a page does to the recent list
notes.body:
The key is right: `[A, B, C]`; A moves to the front and its old entry is removed. `setActivePage` sets `recent` to `[pageId, ...state.recent.filter((id) => id !== pageId)]`, capped with `.slice(0, 40)`. Step by step for `[B, A, C]` and A: the filter removes A, giving `[B, C]`; A is put in front, giving `[A, B, C]`. This is a move-to-front list with no duplicates, holding at most 40 pages.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Pages already listed keep their position": the filter removes the old position.
- "Every visit recorded": the filter prevents duplicates.
- "Visit goes to the end": the new id is placed first.

notes.title: Why a client cannot set the stored updatedAt
notes.body:
The key is right: the server's current time overwrites the client's `meta.updatedAt`. The route builds `meta` as `{ ...(state.meta || {}), workspaceId, updatedAt: new Date().toISOString() }`. In an object literal, a later key wins over an earlier one with the same name. The client's `meta` is spread first, then `updatedAt` is written again with the server's time. So whatever the client sent, including 2099, is replaced. The response also returns this server time.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Rejected with 400": the only 400 check is the basic shape of `pages` and `blocksByPage`; dates are not validated.
- "The later of the two times": there is no comparison; the server time always wins.
- "Stored exactly as sent": the later `updatedAt` key overrides it.

excerpts.quote: return json({ ok: true, updatedAt: nextState.meta.updatedAt });

notes.title: Why dragging a page under its own grandchild does nothing
notes.body:
The key is right: nothing happens, because walking up from C reaches A and the move is refused as a cycle. `movePage(A, C)` first checks whether the new parent is the page itself (it is not), then calls `isDescendant(pages, C, A)`. That function starts at C and follows `parentId` links upward: C's parent is B, B's parent is A. It finds A and returns true, so `movePage` returns `{}`, which changes nothing. Moving A under C would have made A its own ancestor, a loop in the tree.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Throws and shows a toast": the action returns quietly; nothing throws.
- "B is re-parented to the root": no other page is changed.
- "C becomes the new root": again, the action makes no changes at all.
